title: Short Stuff: The Santa Claus Association
summary: Christmas holiday Short Stuff episode on the Santa Claus Association, a New York City charity that answered children's letters to Santa after the U.S. Postal Service's handling of them drew public outrage. Covers the 1907–1911 Postmaster General policy reversals, the Charitable Organization Society's investigations, the 1911 handover to John Duval Gluck Jr., Gluck's fraudulent credentials and genuine charitable work, the association's growth and its Santa Claus building plans, Commissioner Bird Collar's crackdown on unregulated charities, Gluck's departure to Miami, and the later USPS Operation Santa Claus. Based on a History Extra article by Alex Palmer.

segments.title: Christmas greetings and episode setup
segments.summary: The hosts exchange Christmas greetings and gifts, then introduce the Santa Claus Association topic and suggest search terms for finding it.

segments.title: Postal Service destroys letters to Santa
segments.summary: Around the turn of the century, the US Postal Service in New York sent children's letters to Santa to the Dead Letter office. Public outcry led the Postmaster General in 1907 to hand letters to charities, but in 1908 the policy was reversed after the Charitable Organization Society found some letter writers were not as needy as claimed. Public outrage followed.

segments.title: 1911 policy and New York's Santa gap
segments.summary: In 1911 the Postmaster General allowed charities to take letters to Santa. No New York group stepped up for two years, and newspapers reported that Santa was in trouble. Postmaster Edward Morgan then received an offer from John Duval Gluck Jr.

segments.title: Gluck's fake credentials
segments.summary: Gluck, a customs broker with no children who was not married, claimed to be a special newspaper representative, a famous tariff expert and investigator, and a Secret Service member. None of these claims were true; the hosts describe him as a con man.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: The hosts take a short break before continuing the story.

segments.title: Growth of the Santa Claus Association
segments.summary: Gluck created the Santa Claus Association, a bottom-up volunteer effort by New York City residents, clubs and organizations that matched letters with donors. The first year it answered requests from 28,000 children. Gluck kept asking for more money, eventually proposing a Santa Claus building in Manhattan. The hosts link the optimism of the post-World War One and jazz age to the funding.

segments.title: Commissioner Bird Collar's crackdown and Gluck's exit
segments.summary: Commissioner Bird Collar of New York's Public Welfare department investigated unregulated charities, including the Santa Claus Association. Gluck had poor records, so he could not be convicted, but he lost control of the association and the letters and left for Miami. The Santa Claus association headquarters was reportedly in the back of a Manhattan steakhouse. Christmas was becoming more commercial at the time, including the first Macy's Christmas Parade.

segments.title: Operation Santa Claus today
segments.summary: The US Postal Service later started Operation Santa Claus, which the hosts say was partly inspired by Gluck's system. Today a committee of Postal employees runs an app connecting children in need with donors. The hosts credit Alex Palmer's History Extra article as the source.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts wish listeners Merry Christmas and close the short episode with credits.
